seo.title: Judith in the Bible: her story, Holofernes and her book
seo.description: Judith in plain words: the widow who walked into Holofernes' camp to save her town, her prayer and song, which Bibles hold her book, and the myths.

who: Judith was a rich, God-fearing widow of Bethulia, a hill town under siege by the Assyrian general Holofernes. When its rulers promised to surrender in five days, she rebuked them. Then she dressed in her finest clothes, walked into the enemy camp with her maid, and cut off Holofernes' head while he lay drunk. The army fled.

facts.label: In the Bible
facts.text: The **Book of Judith**, 16 chapters. She appears in chapter 8, and the rest of the book is hers.

facts.label: Which Bibles
facts.text: **Catholic** and **Orthodox** Bibles have it. **Protestant** Bibles leave it out, or print it among the **Apocrypha**. It is not in the **Hebrew** Bible.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Bethulia**, a hill town guarding a pass on the way to Jerusalem. No one has found it for sure.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: Daughter of **Merari**, of the tribe of **Simeon**. Widow of **Manasses**, who left her gold, silver, servants, cattle and land. The book names no children.

facts.label: Her name
facts.text: **Yehudit** in Hebrew. It means **Jewess**, a woman of Judah.

facts.label: When
facts.text: The book sets it under **Nebuchadnezzar**, whom it calls king of the Assyrians, soon after the Jews came home from exile. Whether it happened, and when, is argued over: see Her book, below.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: At **Bethulia**, aged **105**. She was buried in her husband's cave, and Israel mourned her seven days.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Righteous Judith**, in the Orthodox Church. **Holy Judith**, in Ambrose.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Nearly always with a **sword**, as in all three pictures on this page. Often her maid is with her, carrying the head of **Holofernes**.

moments.title: A widow on the roof
moments.text: Judith's husband Manasses died at the barley harvest. He had stood in the heat over the men binding sheaves, fell on his bed, and died. For three years and four months she lived as a widow. She made a tent on the roof of her house and wore sackcloth. She fasted every day, except Sabbaths, new moons and feasts. She was beautiful, and rich in land and servants. “No one said anything evil about her, for she feared God exceedingly.”

moments.title: Five days
moments.text: Holofernes, the chief general of Nebuchadnezzar, came to take the hill country. He camped below Bethulia with 170,000 foot soldiers and seized the springs. After 34 days the cisterns were empty. Women and young men fainted from thirst in the streets. The people begged their rulers to surrender. Ozias, the chief ruler, asked them to hold out five more days for God to help. “But if these days pass, and no help comes to us, I will do what you say.”

moments.title: “Who are you?”
moments.text: Judith heard of the oath and sent her maid to fetch the rulers. She told them their word “is not right”. They had set God a deadline, as if He could be threatened. Better to wait for His help, and pray. Ozias answered that she had spoken well, but the oath stood. “And now pray for us, because you are a godly woman.” Judith had another answer. “I will do a thing, which will go down to all generations among the children of our race.” She would not tell them what.

moments.when: The hour of the evening incense
moments.title: Her prayer
moments.text: At the hour when the evening incense was offered in Jerusalem, Judith lay face down, put ashes on her head, and cried out to God. She remembered how He had put a sword in the hand of her forefather Simeon. She asked Him to bless the plan she had made, even its lies: “Strike by the deceit of my lips the servant with the prince”. And she asked for a strange victory. “Break down their arrogance by the hand of a woman.” The heart of her prayer is below, in Her words.

moments.title: The garments of gladness
moments.text: She took off her sackcloth and her widow's clothes. She bathed, anointed herself and braided her hair. She put on the clothes she used to wear while her husband lived, and all her jewellery. Her maid carried wine, oil, roasted grain, figs and bread, so that she would eat nothing unclean in the camp. The elders at the gate were astonished at her beauty. The men of the town watched her go down the mountain and across the valley, until “they could see her no more.”

moments.title: Before Holofernes
moments.text: The Assyrian watch stopped her. She said she had fled her people, and would show Holofernes how to take the hill country without losing a man. A hundred men took her to his tent, and the whole camp came out to stare. She told him her people were about to sin, by eating food set apart for God. Then God would give them into his hand. She would go out each night to pray, and tell him when. Holofernes was delighted. If she did as she said, “your God will be my God”.

moments.title: Nights at the spring
moments.text: Holofernes offered her food from his own table and wine from his own cup. She refused: she would eat what she had brought. She asked leave to go out to pray, and he told his guards not to stop her. For three days she stayed in the camp. Each night she went down to the spring in the valley of Bethulia, washed, and prayed to God to direct her way.

moments.title: The banquet
moments.text: On the fourth day Holofernes gave a feast for his own servants, and sent his eunuch Bagoas to bring her. He had wanted her since the day he saw her. She came in all her finery, and ate and drank what her maid had prepared. Holofernes “drank exceedingly much wine, more than he had drunk at any time in one day since he was born.” When evening came, the guests left and Bagoas shut the tent from outside. Judith was left alone with him. He lay sprawled on his bed, drunk.

moments.title: The sword
moments.text: Standing by the bed, she prayed in her heart. She took his sword down from the bedpost at his head. She took hold of his hair and said, “Strengthen me, O Lord God of Israel, this day.” She struck his neck twice with all her might, and cut off his head. She rolled the body off the bed and took down the canopy. Then she gave the head to her maid, who put it in the food bag. The two walked out of the camp, as they did every night, to pray.

moments.title: “Open, open the gate”
moments.text: From far off she called to the watchmen. “Open, open the gate, now. God is with us”. The whole town ran down, small and great, hardly believing it, and lit a fire to see. She took the head out of the bag and held it up, with the canopy. “The Lord struck him by the hand of a woman.” He had not touched her, she told them. All the people bowed down and worshipped God.

moments.title: The rout
moments.text: At her word they hung the head on the wall. At sunrise the men of the town marched out as if to attack. The Assyrian officers ran to wake their general. Bagoas knocked, went in, and found the body without its head. He tore his clothes and shouted to the army: “One woman of the Hebrews has brought shame upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar”. Panic swept the camp, and the whole army fled. Israel chased them past Damascus, and plundered the camp for thirty days.

moments.title: Her song
moments.text: Joakim the high priest came from Jerusalem to see her and bless her. The women of Israel danced for her, and she led the dance, crowned with olive, with the men following in their armour. Then she sang a song of thanksgiving, and all the people sang with her. “The Almighty Lord brought them to nothing by the hand of a woman.” The people had given her Holofernes' tent and his silver. At Jerusalem she gave it all to God, the canopy too.

words.note: Judith wrote nothing we have. These are her words as her book records them. Her book is not in the Berean Standard Bible, so her lines on this page are from the World English Bible, with capitals for God. The few other Bible lines are from the BSB.

feature.q: For Your power stands not in numbers, nor Your might in strong men, but You are a God of the afflicted. You are a helper of the oppressed, a helper of the weak, a protector of the forsaken, a savior of those who are without hope.
feature.ctx: Her town had five days left. She lay face down, with ashes on her head, at the hour of the evening incense in Jerusalem.

quotes.q: Now who are you that you have tested God this day, and stand in the place of God among the children of men?
quotes.who: To the rulers of Bethulia, who had promised to surrender in five days.

quotes.q: For God is not like a human being, that He should be threatened, neither is He like a son of man, that He should be won over by pleading.

quotes.q: Besides all this let's give thanks to the Lord our God, Who tries us, even as He did our fathers also.

quotes.q: Praise God! Praise Him! Praise God, Who has not taken away His mercy from the house of Israel, but has destroyed our enemies by my hand tonight!

quotes.q: Let all Your creation serve You; for You spoke, and they were made. You sent out Your Spirit, and it built them. There is no one who can resist Your voice.
For all sacrifice is little for a sweet savor, and all the fat is very little for a whole burnt offering to You; but he who fears the Lord is great continually.

myths.claim: Judith slept with Holofernes to get close to him.
myths.truth: Her book says she did not. She dressed to catch his eye, and he meant to seduce her: “He was watching for a time to deceive her from the day that he had seen her.” But he drank himself senseless first. Home again, she swore “he didn't commit sin with me, to defile and shame me.” Only Bagoas, knocking at the tent next morning, “supposed that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith.” Ambrose counts it her first triumph that she came back “with her purity unspotted”.

cite.text: Judith 12:16-20; 13:16; 14:14; Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 3, chapter 13

myths.claim: Judith killed her enemy with a tent peg.
myths.truth: That was Jael, in the book of Judges. While Sisera, the Canaanite general, lay asleep in her tent, Jael drove a tent peg through his temple. Judith used Holofernes' own sword. The two stories have much in common: a woman alone with an enemy general, the general asleep, and a song of praise after.

extras.title: Her book
extras.lede: Judith's whole story is in one book, and Christians have long disagreed about it. Which Bibles hold it, and is it history? Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles
items.text: Early Christians read the book, and Clement of Rome retold her story in his letter to Corinth. Jerome doubted it belonged in Scripture, but translated it anyway, because “the Nicene Council is considered to have counted this book among the number of sacred Scriptures”. A council at Carthage in 419 listed Judith among “the Canonical Scriptures”, and the Council of Trent did the same in 1546. The Orthodox Synod of Jerusalem, in 1672, named Judith among the books it defended:
items.quote: For we judge these also to be with the other genuine Books of Divine Scripture genuine parts of Scripture.

cite.text: Jerome, Preface to Judith, tr. Andrew S. Jacobs; Code of Canons of the African Church (419), canon 24; Council of Trent, fourth session; Confession of Dositheus, question 3, tr. J. Robertson (1899)

items.title: Among the Apocrypha, or left out
items.text: Judith is not in the Hebrew Bible, and Protestant churches follow the Hebrew Bible for their Old Testament. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* puts it plainly: the book “is consequently excluded from the Protestant Canon”. Some Protestant Bibles leave it out. Others print it among the Apocrypha, between the Testaments, where it comes after Tobit. The Church of England's *Thirty-Nine Articles* list “The Book of Judith” among books the Church reads, but not for doctrine. The words, they say, are Jerome's:
items.quote: the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine

cite.text: The Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 6, in the Book of Common Prayer (Oxford, about 1900); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), “Book of Judith”; Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), “Judith, The Book of”

items.title: Not in the Jewish Bible
items.text: Jewish Scripture has never included it. Origen asked the Jews of his day about it in the 200s. Augustine knew that “the Jews are said not to have received” it “into the canon of the Scriptures”. Jerome says the Jews counted it “among the apocrypha”, and he made his Latin from a copy in Aramaic. Origen wrote:
items.quote: Tobias (as also Judith), we ought to notice, the Jews do not use. They are not even found in the Hebrew Apocrypha, as I learned from the Jews themselves.

cite.text: Origen, Letter to Africanus, chapter 13; Augustine, City of God, Book 18, chapter 26; Jerome, Preface to Judith

items.title: A true story
items.text: For most of Christian history the book was read as history. Sulpicius Severus, about 400, tried to find the king under whom she lived, and settled on the Persian Ochus. Augustine placed her story in the time of Cyrus. Defenders point to details a mere story would not need: how her husband died, the passes her town guarded, and a family tree fifteen generations long. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1910 admits “very serious difficulties”. But it says the Fathers “have ever looked upon the book as historical”, and:
items.quote: Catholics with very few exceptions accept the book of Judith as a narrative of facts, not as an allegory.

cite.text: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 14; Augustine, City of God, Book 18, chapter 26; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), “Book of Judith”

items.title: A story told to teach
items.text: Many scholars now read it as a story told to teach, set in a past that never quite was. Its first verse makes Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians at Nineveh. But the Nebuchadnezzar of history ruled from Babylon, after Nineveh had fallen. No one has found Bethulia. And the names can sound like symbols: Judith means Jewess. The scholar R. H. Charles, in the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* of 1911:
items.quote: The book in its fuller form was most probably written in the 2nd century B.C. The writer places his romance two centuries earlier

cite.text: Judith 1:1; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), “Book of Judith”; Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), “Judith, The Book of”

circle.name: Her maid
circle.text: She has no name in the book, but she is at Judith's side from start to end. She carried the food bag into the camp, and carried the head out in it. Judith set her free before she died.

circle.name: Manasses
circle.text: Her husband, of her own tribe and family. He died of the heat at the barley harvest. She lived on in his house, and was buried in his cave.

circle.name: Ozias
circle.text: The chief ruler of Bethulia, of the tribe of Simeon. He promised to surrender after five days, and took her rebuke well: “All that you have spoken, you have spoken with a good heart.”

circle.name: Holofernes
circle.text: The chief general of Nebuchadnezzar, “second to himself”, sent to punish the nations of the west. He laid siege to Bethulia and cut off its water.

circle.name: Bagoas
circle.text: The eunuch in charge of all Holofernes had. He brought Judith to the banquet, shut the tent on the two of them, and found his master dead in the morning.

circle.name: Achior
circle.text: An Ammonite leader who warned Holofernes that Israel could not be beaten unless it sinned against its God. For that, Holofernes had him left bound at the foot of Bethulia's hill. When he saw the head, he fainted. Then he believed in God, was circumcised, and was “joined to the house of Israel”.

circle.name: Joakim
circle.text: The high priest in Jerusalem. He ordered the towns to hold the mountain passes, and came with the elders to bless her after the victory.

death.big: She died at home in Bethulia, at 105, and was buried in her husband's cave.
paras: After the victory she went up to Jerusalem with the people, and stayed three months while they feasted before the temple. Then she went home to her own land, and was honoured “in all the land”.

“Many desired her, but no man knew her all the days of her life” after Manasses died. She grew old in her husband's house. Before she died, she set her maid free, and shared out her goods among her husband's family and her own.

They buried her in the cave of Manasses. “The house of Israel mourned for her seven days.” The book ends on the peace she left behind: “There was no one who made the children of Israel afraid any more in the days of Judith, nor for a long time after her death.”

saint.big: The Orthodox honour her as **Righteous Judith**, on the Sunday of the Forefathers in December. No Western church keeps a day for her.

churches.note: Sunday of the Forefathers, in December
Her book is in its Bible
Her song is a Church of England canticle

paras: Rome's 1916 book of martyrs has no day for her, and the Anglican and Lutheran calendars have none either. Yet the Fathers called her holy: Ambrose writes of “holy Judith”. And the Church of England sings her song. *Common Worship: Daily Prayer* keeps it among its canticles, as A Song of Judith.

The OCA lists **Righteous Judith** on the **Sunday of the Forefathers**, the Sunday between 11 and 17 December, when the Orthodox remember the righteous of the Old Testament. Of her it says only this:

quotes.q: Information about the Righteous Judith may be found in the Old Testament book bearing her name.
quotes.who: The OCA, on the Sunday of the Forefathers

kin.name: Deborah
kin.text: A prophetess who judged Israel. She foretold that an enemy general would fall to a woman: “the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.”

kin.name: Esther
kin.text: Clement of Rome praises her in the same breath as Judith. She too risked her life to save her people: “And if I perish, I perish!”

kin.name: Abigail
kin.text: “An intelligent and beautiful woman” who rode out with bread, wine and figs to meet an armed man, and turned him back with her words.
